title: Master Class | The Queen's Gambit | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: In the Accepted there are two fundamentally different roads — the solid one built around a modest pawn move, or the aggressive central grab with e4. The big centre isn't the only move, or even the main one, but it's considered the most testing.
The rook-pawn move is odd — it just lets the pawn be recaptured, and in this line every tempo matters. Facing passive play, there's nothing exotic to do; simply develop the pieces cleanly.

Follow your instincts — capturing would only invite a queen trade, so the obvious move is to push to d5, grabbing more of the centre and building tension. If it's exchanged, a knight lands on a beautiful central outpost.

A very instructive moment — many players see the knight tension and assume they must react, breaking the position or lunging the queen out. It's a false alarm: nothing is actually threatened. A capture is met by recapturing with the bishop, which is just as good, and grabbing the central pawn would be catastrophic, opening the file for a rook and a decisive pin. So develop as if nothing happened, because nothing did.

The opponent blunders — spot the standoff, the two queens facing off with the king tied to defending its own. Distract that defender with the classic bishop check on f7, and the queen falls. A queen guarded by only one piece is always susceptible to exactly this kind of shot.

Do run the safety check first — after the king takes, make sure there's no in-between check that saves the defender. Here that resource is blocked by the opponent's own pawn, so the queen is simply won and the game with it.

The solid pawn move hides a trap over four hundred years old — if the opponent tries to hold the extra pawn with a queenside advance, undermine the base of that pawn chain with the rook-pawn. Attack the foundation and the whole structure trembles.

If the defender props the pawn with the c-pawn, a further break opens the diagonal, and a queen swing to f3 wins a piece or the rook — because, absurd as it looks, the rook simply can't be defended. A famous position that has stood the test of centuries.

The principled reply is the counter-thrust to e5 — and it's a counter-gambit, because capturing it lets the queens come off with a check that strips the castling rights and leaves the king exposed. With the material level again, that's simply bad for the first player.

So instead the knight develops, and after the exchanges the gambit spirit is preserved — down a pawn, but two pieces out against none, with pressure bearing down on f7. The line equalises for the defender only with great precision; anyone who hasn't studied it gets swept away.

A closing lesson on choosing openings — modelling your repertoire on the elite often backfires, because they can violate the rules only after years of study. For anyone with less time, pick lines where forgetting a move order doesn't get you blown off the board. Forgiving beats fashionable.
